reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: A subungual haematoma is a collection of blood beneath the nail plate, usually following acute trauma such as a crush injury or repetitive pressure
Acute lesions cause throbbing pain from pressure of the trapped blood, which appears as a red-black discolouration under the plate
Painful acute haematomas can be relieved by trephination (making a small hole in the nail) to drain the blood
Over time the pigment moves distally with nail growth and can be seen to advance, unlike a fixed melanocytic band
The main diagnostic concern is distinguishing a haematoma from a subungual melanoma, particularly when there is no clear history of trauma
Onychoscopy typically shows a homogeneous reddish-black colour with a globular or streaky periphery and, often, a filamentous distal edge, helping separate it from melanoma
A significant crush injury may be associated with an underlying phalangeal fracture or nail bed laceration, which should be assessed and managed appropriately
reference.pathophysiology: A subungual haematoma forms when trauma ruptures the vessels of the nail bed or matrix and blood accumulates in the confined space between the plate and the bed. The rigid nail plate prevents the blood from escaping, so pressure builds and causes the characteristic throbbing pain of an acute lesion. As the nail grows the trapped pigment is carried distally and eventually grows out, which distinguishes it from melanin deposited continuously by matrix melanocytes. A forceful crush mechanism can simultaneously fracture the underlying distal phalanx or lacerate the nail bed, so the haematoma may be a marker of deeper injury.
additionalDifferentials: Longitudinal melanonychia from a benign source
additionalInvestigations: History of trauma and the time course of the discolouration
Onychoscopy to identify features favouring haematoma over melanoma
Serial observation to confirm distal migration of pigment with nail growth
Radiograph after significant trauma to exclude an underlying phalangeal fracture
Assessment of the nail bed for laceration in acute crush injuries
Nail matrix or bed biopsy if pigment persists or melanoma cannot be excluded
redFlags: Pigmented subungual lesion without a convincing history of trauma, raising concern for melanoma
Pigment that fails to migrate distally or grow out over time
Associated Hutchinson sign or nail dystrophy suggesting malignancy
Significant crush injury with suspected phalangeal fracture or extensive nail bed laceration
Signs of secondary infection following trauma or trephination
reference.prognosis: A simple traumatic subungual haematoma resolves as it grows out with the nail and has an excellent outcome, but a mistaken diagnosis that overlooks a subungual melanoma can have serious consequences, so persistent or unexplained pigment must be pursued.
pitfalls: Attributing a pigmented lesion to trauma without a clear history and missing a melanoma
Failing to confirm distal migration of the pigment over follow-up
Overlooking an underlying fracture or nail bed laceration after a crush injury
Not offering trephination for a painful acute haematoma when it would relieve pressure
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Decompress a painful acute haematoma involving a large fraction of the nail by trephination to release the trapped blood
Offer simple analgesia and elevation for smaller or resolving lesions
Obtain a radiograph after significant crush trauma to exclude an underlying distal phalangeal fracture
Remove the nail plate and repair the nail bed where there is extensive laceration or a displaced fracture, giving tetanus prophylaxis for open wounds
Confirm a benign course by observing distal migration of pigment as the nail grows out
Perform nail matrix or bed biopsy if the pigment persists or melanoma cannot be excluded
Recommend well-fitting footwear and activity modification for recurrent traumatic toenail lesions
